Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go. That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our interviews should evolve, too. page.text_excerpt: SKIP TO CONTENT SKIP TO SITE INDEX SECTION NAVIGATION Search U.S. LOG IN Justice Antonin Scalia, 2008 Sir William Blackstone, 1769 A Supreme Court decision in 2008 case incorrectly quoted a centuries-old legal treatise, with profound implications for today’s gun-control laws. How a Misquote by a Supreme Court Justice Imperils Gun Restrictions By Mike McIntire and Eli Murray Nov. 10, 2026 Share full article When the Supreme Court begins weighing the constitutionality of assault-weapons bans next month, the justices will be guided by the court’s own precedent: a landmark ruling that such restrictions are allowed only if a firearm is both “dangerous and unusual.” For nearly two decades, judges across the country have invoked this language to strike down gun-control laws. It is a pivotal legal test. It is also based on a misquote. Justice Antonin Scalia, writing for the majority in the 2008 case, District of Columbia v. Heller, attributed the “dangerous and unusual” language to Sir William Blackstone, an 18th-century English jurist whose writings became the basis for much of American law. But in his seminal 1769 treatise, “Commentaries on the Laws of England,” Blackstone referred to weapons that were “dangerous or unusual,” suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted. The consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of “and” rather than “or” have been profound. Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity. A New York Times review found that courts have applied the “dangerous and unusual” test in at least 98 opinions in civil lawsuits that challenged weapons restrictions, most of them bankrolled by activist groups, since the 2008 Heller decision. Much of that hardware does one of two jobs: training new models or running finished ones to answer requests from millions of people around the world. A supercomputer is built from many of the same parts but for a different purpose. It is typically owned by a government lab or university and designed for scientific simulation, such as modeling climate, nuclear physics, or new materials. That work demands high-precision math and very fast communication between processors. Rather than serving the masses, a supercomputer is shared among researchers, whose large jobs wait in a queue and run according to a schedule. Early examples like UNIVAC and the IBM 7030 were used by scientists working on atomic research. The Cray-1 came along in the mid-70s and accelerated such work to new levels. Each of these machines brought with it new technologies that made those breakthroughs possible. They were also fairly bespoke, built of components regular nerds could only dream about. Over time, that changed. By the time the 1990s rolled around, companies like Cray saw their hardware being outpaced by newcomers who were packing far more processors into their products. The kicker?
